report:
## Conclusion

The claim that soursop (graviola, Annona muricata) "cures cancer in humans" is **not supported by scientific evidence** and should be considered false or, at best, unproven.

Laboratory (in vitro) and some animal studies have shown that compounds in soursop—particularly acetogenins like annonacin—can kill certain cancer cells or slow tumor growth in petri dishes and rodents. This has fueled widespread internet claims and folk use, especially in Latin America, Africa, and the Caribbean. However, no controlled human clinical trials have ever demonstrated that soursop cures or effectively treats cancer in people. Major cancer authorities, including Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Cancer Research UK, explicitly state there is no reliable clinical evidence supporting its use as a cancer treatment (Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop). Fact-checking organizations have repeatedly debunked viral claims to this effect (PolitiFact, https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/; Snopes, https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/).

There are also safety concerns: annonacin, the key bioactive compound studied for anticancer potential, is a known mitochondrial toxin linked to neurotoxicity and an atypical form of Parkinson's disease with chronic consumption (PubMed, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/14521988/). This raises risk without proven benefit.

**Bottom line:** Promising lab findings do not equal a cure. Relying on soursop instead of evidence-based cancer treatment could be dangerous, potentially delaying effective care and introducing neurotoxic risk. Patients should consult oncologists rather than substitute conventional treatment with soursop.
